learningObjective: Put VMs in availability sets or zones. Explain fault domains and update domains. Match each option to the failures it survives and its SLA.
engineer: Availability set: spreads VMs across racks in one datacenter.
Fault domains: groups of racks that share power and network. Up to 3 (2 or 3, depending on the region). If one fails, VMs in the others keep running.
Update domains: groups that Azure restarts one at a time during planned maintenance. Up to 20 (default 5).
Availability set tips: use the Aligned SKU for managed disks, so disks follow the fault domains. SLA: 99.95% for two or more VMs in a set.

Availability zones: separate buildings in one region, each with its own power, cooling and network. Put VMs in different zones (zones: ['1'], ['2'], ['3']). Use services that also span zones: Standard Load Balancer, Standard public IP, and ZRS disks where supported. SLA: 99.99% for two or more VMs across two or more zones.
Single VM SLA: 99.9%, if all its disks are Premium SSD, Premium SSD v2 or Ultra (lower for other disk types).
Rules: you choose the availability set when you create the VM. You can't add an existing VM to a set; recreate it from its disks. A VM can't be in both a set and a zone.
Scale sets: a Flexible scale set spreads VMs across zones and fault domains for you.
Neither protects a whole region: for that, copy to a second region with Azure Site Recovery.
Proximity placement groups: put VMs physically close for low latency. The trade-off: they are less spread out.

example.title: Picking the right option for two apps
body: An intranet app that can tolerate some downtime runs on two VMs in an availability set (99.95%). A customer checkout service runs three VMs across zones, behind a zone-redundant Standard Load Balancer (99.99%).
Both teams also copy their VMs to the paired region with Site Recovery, because neither option survives a whole region going down.

architectureDecisions: Important apps use zones: when the region has them.
Spread everything, not just VMs: use zone-redundant load balancers and storage too.
Add a second region: for disaster recovery.

misconceptions.myth: An availability set protects you if a datacenter fails.
misconceptions.reality: No. It only spreads VMs across racks inside one datacenter.

misconceptions.myth: One VM in a zone gets 99.99%.
misconceptions.reality: No. 99.99% needs two or more VMs across zones.

comparisons.difference: EC2 spread placement groups are like availability sets. Deploying across AZs is like Azure zones.
Spread VMs across zones and fault domains automatically, and add autoscale.

troubleshooting.symptom: You can't add an existing VM to an availability set.
troubleshooting.cause: The set is chosen when the VM is created.
troubleshooting.fix: Recreate the VM in the set, from its disks.

troubleshooting.symptom: Allocation failure when adding VMs to a set.
troubleshooting.cause: The hardware cluster has no room for that size.
troubleshooting.fix: Deallocate all VMs and start them together, or pick another size.

troubleshooting.cause: The region or size doesn't support zones.
troubleshooting.fix: Pick a region and size that support zones.

configuration.limits: Up to 3 fault domains and 20 update domains

configuration.prerequisites: A region with availability zones (for zones)
A load balancer to share traffic
